name: Jonathan Swift
role: Anglo-Irish satirist, clergyman and pamphleteer, Dean of St Patrick's, Dublin (1667–1745)
summary: Swift described himself as a Whig on the constitution and a Tory on the church. He defended limited monarchy, a supreme representative legislature and government by consent, and an established church with bishops and a test for office. He wrote in defence of Irish liberties against English rule and held that the wealthy owe charity.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He laments the abolition of the House of Lords in the 1640s and attacks Whigs for wanting bishops out of the Lords.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: His Project proposes salaried reviewers to strike offensive passages from stage plays, as the stage corrupts the young; he speaks only of plays.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Sentiments holds episcopacy most agreeable to primitive institution and says a Church of England man would defend it by arms against all powers except the legislature.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Drapier's Letter IV says in reason all government without the consent of the governed is the very definition of slavery, and Letter VI that freedom is being governed by laws made with one's own consent.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He holds no form of government more acceptable to God than another and praises the English limited monarchy as the best constitution.

more-religion-public.rationale: His Project for the Advancement of Religion urges the Crown to use patronage and the court to make piety a condition of preferment and public life.

national-church-status.rationale: He tolerates other worship but would give offices of trust and profit only to those who preserve the established church, and defends the Sacramental Test.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: His sermon On Mutual Subjection calls a rich man who withholds bounty and charity a nuisance in the commonwealth.

parliament-supreme.rationale: He states that in all government there is an absolute unlimited legislative power, in England the King, Lords and Commons, and that whatever it enacts is law; the freedom of a nation lies in such a representative legislature.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: He condemns entering a party with resigned obedience to leaders as unsuited to civil and religious liberty.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: He says party leaders on each side set their hearts on getting or keeping employments rather than the public good, but he speaks of leaders, not most politicians.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: He says the ends of government are met where person and property are secured by laws only the whole can repeal, and he ranks arbitrary power as worse than anarchy.

property-fundamental.rationale: He names the security of person and property by laws only the whole can repeal as the great end of government.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: He calls it a scandal to government to allow unlimited publication against Christian doctrine and says publishers answer for the effects of such opinions.

reason-over-faith.rationale: His sermon On the Trinity says people should not rest so much on their own reason in religion, and that faith in what is above reason is the great virtue.

religion-illusion.rationale: He presents Christianity as true and warns against those who hold it false; he does not treat its comfort as illusory.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: He wants the established Church of England legally favoured, with dissenters tolerated but excluded from office.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: He argues a tyrant like Nero could not be left unresisted in a limited monarchy and defends the Revolution, though he declines to settle whether a king of England may be deposed.

rule-by-example.rationale: He says a good prince's bare example will not reform an age and that rulers must also use preferment and penalties.

separate-church-state.rationale: He defends an established church tied to the constitution, with public office reserved for its communicants.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: He says anyone defending absolute power in a single person should be treated as the common enemy of mankind, and that a prince who is answerable to none but God makes limited monarchy meaningless.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: He regards atheism and writings against revealed religion as a scandal that government should not permit, so state promotion of it contradicts his position.

notes: Themes searched in Swift's prose: religion and church, government and the constitution, toleration and the test, Ireland and the Drapier's Letters, wealth and charity, party, standing armies and war. Satires and fiction (Gulliver, Modest Proposal, Tale of a Tub) were not used as his positions. Ireland economic tracts were not decisive for any statement. Swift's volume 5 English political tracts are not in the local library, and the Conduct of the Allies was not read, so war and alliance statements stay null. Fails or is thin on many lines; left as an honest result.
